reason: The sources provide over a dozen cross-verified facts across multiple sites detailing the 1989 close encounter, discovery circumstances, and impact risks of 4581 Asclepius.
story: In late March 1989, a 300-meter asteroid designated 4581 Asclepius swept past Earth at a distance of about 425,000 miles, nearly twice the distance to the Moon. The encounter was an extraordinarily close shave on cosmic scales, yet no one on Earth knew it occurred in real time. Astronomers Henry Holt and Norman Thomas only spotted the asteroid on March 31, 1989, using the Palomar Observatory—nine full days after its closest approach. Had the Apollo-class space rock collided with Earth, scientists estimate it would have unleashed the explosive equivalent of a 600-megaton nuclear blast, carving massive craters and generating devastating tsunamis. The delayed realization that a city-killing asteroid had flown past completely undetected served as a profound wake-up call, prompting government mandates and space agencies to build dedicated near-Earth object tracking networks and planetary defense programs.
angle: A 1,000-foot city-killing asteroid flew right past Earth in March 1989, and humanity had no idea until astronomers spotted it nine days later.

claims.claim: Asteroid 4581 Asclepius was assigned the provisional designation 1989 FC.
4581 Asclepius is classified as an Apollo-group near-Earth asteroid.
Asclepius is classified as a potentially hazardous asteroid (PHA).
The asteroid was discovered on March 31, 1989.
The asteroid was discovered by astronomers Henry Holt and Norman Thomas.
Asclepius was discovered using telescopes at Palomar Observatory in California.
Asclepius is named after the Greek god of healing and medicine.
In March 1989, Asclepius passed Earth at a distance of approximately 425,000 miles (684,000 kilometers).
The flyby distance was roughly twice the distance from Earth to the Moon.
Asclepius was discovered nine days after its closest approach to Earth.
Astronomer Henry Holt described the asteroid encounter as a close call on the cosmic scale.
An impact from Asclepius was calculated to release energy comparable to a 600-megaton atomic explosion.
Asclepius has an estimated diameter of approximately 300 meters (1,000 feet).
An ocean impact from an asteroid of this scale could trigger devastating tsunamis.
The undetected close encounter spurred government mandates and tracking efforts to monitor dangerous near-Earth objects.
Asclepius will make another close pass within roughly 1.84 million kilometers of Earth in March 2051.
Asclepius completes one orbit around the Sun in approximately 1.03 years.
The absolute magnitude (H) of asteroid 4581 Asclepius is approximately 20.7.

disputed: The exact date of closest approach in March 1989 is listed as March 22 in S1 and S4, but cited as March 23 in S5; scripts should state March 22 or generally refer to late March 1989.

Impact severity ranges from regional metropolitan devastation and localized crop disruption (S3, S4) to full global extinction of life (S5); scripts should attribute global extinction claims to extreme worst-case hyperbole and stick to regional devastation models.
